list.listitem: Based on data from the 1960’s, acute rheumatic fever (ARF) attack rate following an episode of untreated GAS pharyngitis is between 0.3% and 3%; this likely depends, in part, on virulence factors and genetic predisposition. C
Treatment of preceding group A streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis with antibiotics helps prevent 70% to 80% of cases of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). B
An echocardiography with Doppler should be performed in all patients with confirmed or suspected ARF. B
Treatment of carditis often includes corticosteroids and IV immunoglobulin; these have not been proven effective, although the quality of studies is poor. B

Long-term penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrent rheumatic fever attacks and progressive cardiac valvular damage. Intramuscular (IM) regimens are more effective than oral. More frequent dosing schedules (every 3 weeks vs. every 4 weeks) should be considered in endemic areas and in high-risk individuals. B

background.definition: ARF is an illness characterized by inflammatory lesions of the heart (rheumatic heart disease [RHD]), joints, subcutaneous tissue, and central nervous system. When it occurs, ARF invariably follows an episode of GAS pharyngitis.

list.listitem: Worldwide: 470,000 new cases each year.
United States: 0.5/100,000 each year (white, suburban schoolchildren).
Australia: 150 to 380 per 100,000 (primarily Indigenous population in Northern Territory, 5- to 14-year-olds).
Italy: 3.2 to 9.6/100 000 children; incidence increased by 20% using high-risk criteria per 2015 revised Jones criteria, identifying 28 additional patients.
Worldwide, there are an estimated 15 to 19 million cases of RHD, including over 2 million children.

Authors of a systematic review of 2015 data found a higher rate, with a global prevalence of 33.4 million (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 29.7-43.1 million) cases of RHD and 10.5 million (95% UI 9.6-11.5 million) disability-adjusted life-years due to RHD.
Higher prevalence is seen in developing countries of Middle East, South America, India, and Africa (e.g., 12.6/1000 in Zambia).
RHD prevalence in developing countries as defined by abnormal echocardiography may be much higher (21-30/1000).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 82 echocardiograhic screening studies with over 1 million participants found RHD pooled prevalence rates of 26.1% (95% CI 19.2-33.1) and 11.3% (95% CI 7.2-16.2) for studies using the World Heart Federation and World Health Organization criteria, respectively.
Annual cost of ARF in Brazil was estimated to be over 50 million dollars; ARF is even a larger problem in Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.

Authors of a scoping review including 6 papers found that cost estimates varied greatly across countries, perspectives and costing endpoints. US dollar costs for ARF treatment ranged from $6200 per episode for a non-indigenous child to $9700 for an indigenous adult; for secondary prophylaxis, costs ranged from $1300 to $1500. Costs per patient for acute medical management of an RHD episode ranged from $5800 for a non-indigenous child to $8800 for an indigenous child and RHD surgery costs ranged from $46,000 for a non-indigenous adult to $56,000 for an indigenous child.
Most common cause of pediatric heart disease in the world; ARF incidence highest among children aged 5 to 15 years according to the CDC.
In developing countries, most common cause of cardiac mortality among those under 40 years.

Estimated 490,000 deaths/year worldwide due to RHD; deaths in United States: 3248 in 2004. Estimated global deaths/year from RHD were lower in 2015 at 319,400 (95% UI 297,300-337,300) based on a systematic review, although there were large regional differences.

In the US, between 1980 and 2014 there were 355,711 deaths from RHD over a period of 34 years, with a decrease of 51.9% (95% UI 49.2%-54.4%) between 1980 and 2014, although rates increased in two counties in Louisiana. The highest age-standardized mortality rates were in counties clustered in Alaska, Mississippi, Alabama, Kentucky, and Utah, with smaller clusters found in Georgia, South Carolina, and South Dakota. The lowest rates were clustered in western Washington, southern California, and Arizona, the Texas border with Mexico, central Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, southern Florida, Maryland, southern New York state, New Jersey, and Rhode Island.
In less developed countries, RHD is the leading cause of stroke in the young.
Preceding upper respiratory infection with "immunologically significant" serotype of GAS; usually a delayed sequela of 1 to 5 weeks following pharyngitis due to S. pyogenes.

This concept has been challenged by authors of a systematic review of papers reporting GAS emm-type or emm-type-specific antibody responses associated with RF. Of 411 cases of RF identified, 73 different emm types were associated with RF with the classic rheumatogenic emm types representing only 12.3% of the emm types and responsible for roughly one third (31.6%) of the clinical cases. Knowledge of emm clusters will likely help in vaccine development.

Genetic susceptibility is also reported, with limited data showing TGF-β1 [rs1800469] and and IL-1β [rs2853550] single nucleotide polymorphisms contributing to RHD susceptibility. Authors of a meta-analysis found an association between cytokine gene polymorphisms and susceptibility to RHD in patients with ARF.
An autoimmune response is theorized to be responsible for ARF.
"T cell mimicry"-cross-reactivity between streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin has been described.
Continued live GAS may play a role in ARF/RHD pathogenesis.
Delayed hypersensitivity responses to strep antigens and genetic predisposition (HLA sites) may also be important factors.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Barriers to accessing primary health care

list.listitem: Primary prevention is to detect and treat strep pharyngitis with antibiotics to prevent ARF. B

Secondary prevention is long-term penicillin prophylaxis to prevent recurrent RF attacks and progressive cardiac valvular damage. IM regimens are more effective than oral and every 2- to 3-week intervals are better than every 4 weeks. B
No universal screening for RHD is recommended in developed countries.

A study examining universal echocardiographic screening for RHD found much higher prevalence (10-fold) in developing countries, which suggests a role for echocardiographic screening in endemic areas. Authors of the systematic review and meta-analysis, reported above, also found that prevalence rates varied inversely with a countries’ income.

Simplified echocardiography screening using mitral regurgitation jet-length criteria may improve detection of RHD in children in low-income countries. Interestingly, health-related quality of life (HRQOL) was reduced for children in Uganda who screened positive for latent RHD despite lack of symptoms compared to children who screened negative; linkage to medical care may mitigate the reduction in HRQOL.
Trained nurses or medical students can be successful in conducting echocardiographic screening.

Detection and appropriate treatment of GAS pharyngitis can prevent ARF. Estimated ARF reduction is by about two-thirds within two months (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.26-0.50; 18 studies, 12,249 participants; moderate‐certainty evidence), although overall prevalence of acute RF is very low.

Authors of a study of evaluating strategies for testing and treatment for patients with uncomplicated sore throat determined that the optimal strategy for patients at high-risk for ARF, based on prevalence of RHD in the community, should be testing with a point-of-care test and prescribing antibiotics for those who test positive. This strategy would result in 19-22% of patients being treated and no patients harboring GAS going untreated. For low-risk patients, only providing antibiotics to patients with more than low pain levels despite adequate analgesia, Centor scores of 3-4 (or 2–3 FeverPAIN scores or 3–4 McIsaac scores) and a POCT confirming the presence of GABHS is the optimal strategy. This strategy would require testing in only 10–15% of patients and prescribing antibiotics to only 3.5–6.6%.

Authors of a Cochrane review examining different antibiotic choices were uncertain if there were clinically relevant differences between antibiotics for GAS compared with penicillin (penicillin 250-500 mg twice daily for 10 days is still considered first-line therapy); cephalosporins can be considered first-line in adults with relapse (NNT to benefit 50).
However, one-third of ARF episodes follow asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic cases of strep pharyngitis.

In a RCT of 53 schools, use of a school-based sore-throat clinic for diagnosis and treatment of GAS pharyngitis did not prevent cases of ARF compared with usual care in a high-risk setting in Australia.
Vaccine trials are being carried out, but a GAS vaccine is not currently approved.
Careful history to identify patients with previous ARF episode.

Continued prophylaxis with (preferred option) IM benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks (consider every 3 weeks in areas of greater prevalence). Alternatives to injections: oral penicillin V, oral sulfadiazine, erythromycin. See "Drug treatment" for dosing.

Subcutaneous (SC) administration of benzathine penicillin G may be an additional alternative to IM regimens. In a phase I study in health males, the principal absorption half-life of SC benzathine penicillin G was 20.1 (16.3-29.5) days compared with 10.2 (8.6-12.5) days following IM administration. Lower peak and higher trough penicillin concentrations resulted following SC injection.

The American Heart Association (AHA) recommends that where there is uncertainty about a RF diagnosis, it is reasonable to consider offering 12 months of secondary prophylaxis followed by reevaluation to include a careful history and physical examination in addition to a repeat echocardiogram.

Endocarditis prophylaxis is recommended for prevention of complications in patients with residual valvular disease, as per the updated American College of Chest Physicians Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines.

As there is no single sign, symptom, or laboratory test that confirms the diagnosis of RF, application of the revised (2015) Jones Criteria () is the clinical diagnostic standard, especially for initial episodes. B

In patients with clinical carditis confirmed by echocardiography OR arthritis OR subcutaneous nodules OR erythema marginatum, diagnose ARF using another major or 2 minor criteria. Patients with arthritis OR chorea AND clinical or subclinical carditis on echocardiography can also be diagnosed with ARF.
World Health Organization and AHA criteria (based on the Jones criteria) can be used to diagnose recurrent as well as initial episodes of rheumatic fever. C
Echocardiography with Doppler should be performed in all patients with confirmed and suspected ARF. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually no valvular involvement; positive RF (adults)
Positive ANA, anti-DS DNA, malar rash
History of new medication or biologic agent
History of sickle disease per newborn screen, peripheral smear
Positive blood cultures (but can coexist with RHD), heart murmur, positive ECG
Lack of valvular abnormalities on ECG
History of tick bite; erythema migrans, antibody test
Elevated uric acid; urate crystals in synovial fluid

list.listitem: See for the revised Jones criteria.

To diagnose presumptive recurrent RF, a patient should have a reliable past history of ARF or established RHD, documented GAS infection, and 2 major or 1 major and 2 minor or 3 minor manifestations. When minor manifestations alone are present, the exclusion of other more likely causes of the clinical presentation is recommended before a diagnosis of an ARF recurrence is made.
WHO criteria address recurrences as well.
An Australian/New Zealand guideline for the diagnosis of ARF is also available (2012). The guideline uses subclinical (echocardiographic) carditis as a major criterion.

Most patients with ARF have a history of recent strep pharyngitis in the past 1 to 5 weeks (average 19 days), a positive throat culture, or a rapid antigen test. However, one study found this occurred in only 30% of RF cases in a high-prevalence area.

The most common major manifestations during a first episode of ARF are carditis and arthritis. Carditis (primarily valvulitis) occurs in 40% to 70% and is characterized by a new apical systolic murmur, radiating to the aaxilla (mitral regurgitation) or basal diastolic murmur (aortic regurgitation). Polyarthritis (37%-66%) is usually migratory with redness, warmth, and limited range of motion of larger joints (knees, ankles).

Sydenham's chorea occurs in 10% to 40% and involves purposeless, involuntary, rapid movements of the trunk and/or extremities; longer latent period (up to several months) compared with other manifestations.

Erythema marginatum occurs in less than 6% and consists of migratory skin lesions with pale centers and serpiginous borders occurring on the trunk and extremities. Subcutaneous nodules occur in more than 10% and are firm, painless nodules on extensor surfaces and over the spine; they accompany carditis.
Cardiac auscultation of a murmur has poor sensitivity and positive predictive value compared with echocardiography for detection of RHD.
Presentation varies with age: younger patients present more often with carditis and older patients with arthritis.
Occurs rarely before age 5 years, but those patients present more often with moderate to severe carditis and erythema marginatum.

If ARF is suspected, order an ASO titer and ECG. An ASO titer over 200 is seen in 80% of patients with ARF and seen in 90% if 2 specimens are obtained within 2 months of onset. Consider anti-DNase-B if ASO is negative or equivocal; titer may be elevated for several months after GAS infection.

The AHA notes that evidence of preceding strep infection can be confirmed if a patient has a positive throat culture for GAS, a child whose clinical presentation suggests a high pretest probability of streptococcal pharyngitis has a positive rapid GAS antigen test, or there is an increased or rising ASO titer or other streptococcal antibodies (anti-DNASE B).

Authors of a systematic review of usefulness of GAS antibodies for ARF diagnosis found an odds ratio (OR) for elevated SLO titers of 10.57, 95% CI 3.36-33.29 (10 studies) and for DNAse B of 6.97, 95% CI 2.99-16.27 (7 studies). Sensitivity might be improved by increasing the number of GAS proteins in the test.
Can repeat throat culture, but infection versus colonization can be confusing.

ESR and CRP are nonspecific but confirm acute inflammatory state; these can be normal in patients with chorea alone. Complement factors may also be useful; authors of one study reported linked an IgG3-C4 response as important in the initial inflammatory stage of ARF which may have utility as a clinical biomarker.

An echocardiogram with Doppler should be performed in all patients with confirmed or suspected ARF. Findings not consistent with carditis should allow exclusion of that diagnosis in patients with a heart murmur otherwise thought to indicate rheumatic carditis.
Serial echocardiography/Doppler studies should be considered in any patient with diagnosed or suspected ARF even if documented carditis is not present on diagnosis.

Echocardiographic criteria for RHD have been developed by the World Heart Federation. These define RHD morphologic features and criteria for pathological mitral and aortic regurgitation resulting in cases being classified as definite RHD, borderline RHD, or normal. Specific echocardiographic criteria for the diagnosis of carditis are also listed by the AHA and American Society of Echocardiography.

Hand-held echocardiography can be used for RHD screening. Based on a meta-analysis of five studies comparing hand-held to standard echocardiography, authors found a sensitivity of 91.06% (80.46%-100%) and specificity of 91.96% (85.57%-98.36%) for the detection of definite RHD and sensitivity of 62.01% (31.80%-92.22%) and specificity of 82.33% (65.15%-99.52%) for the detection of borderline RHD.
There is no definitive single diagnostic test for ARF, so it is important to exclude other possibilities in the differential diagnosis (see "Differential diagnosis").

Suspect ARF in patients who present with fever, migratory joint pain, and carditis (e.g., tachycardia, murmur, friction rub) following an episode of strep pharyngitis and apply the Jones criteria for diagnosis ().
Jones criteria are most applicable to an initial attack of ARF. WHO criteria are available that also address recurrences.

In high-risk individuals (especially in developing countries), echocardiography was shown to increase diagnostic sensitivity; valvular abnormalities on echocardiography are a major criterion in the Australian/New Zealand guideline and as a recommendation by the AHA.
Goals of treatment of rheumatic fever are to suppress inflammation, eradicate GAS pharyngeal infection, manage heart failure, and prevent progressive valvular disease due to recurrences. C
Although corticosteroids and IV immunoglobulin therapy are used to treat active carditis, they have not been proven effective regarding prevention of valvular disease. B

IM penicillin regimens for secondary prevention are more effective than oral at preventing recurrences. Dosing schedules of every 2 to 3 weeks are better than every 4 weeks and should be considered in high-prevalence areas and high-risk individuals. B

Goals of ARF treatment are to resolve GAS pharyngitis (if active), reduce inflammation (of carditis and arthritis), control heart failure, and prevent recurrences (which cause progressive valve disease).
GAS pharyngitis treatment is presented elsewhere. Eradication of GAS during ARF, however, has never been proved to affect cardiac outcome at one year.

Standard anti-inflammatory therapy is aspirin. Adults: 4 to 8 g/d orally divided every 4 to 6 hours; Children: 80 to 100 mg/kg/d divided every 4 to 6 hours. Check serum levels to maintain 20 to 25 mg/dL, wean slowly over 4 to 6 weeks.

Corticosteroids and IV immunoglobulin: recommended by some authorities if carditis is present but there is no conclusive proof of improved cardiac outcomes and no new trials since 2001. Consider consultation with cardiology and infectious disease if these therapies are being considered. Steroids may decrease symptom duration in patients with chorea.

Secondary prevention with long-term prophylactic doses of antibiotics is the most effective way of preventing RHD. Recommended regimen is benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million U IM every 4 weeks (every 3 weeks in high-risk areas). Oral alternative is penicillin V 250 mg twice daily (less effective). For patients who are penicillin allergic, consider erythromycin 250 mg twice daily.

A Ugandan study screened over 100,000 children and identified 3327 with latent RHD. They randomized 818 to benzylpenicillin every 4 weeks for 2 years or no prophylaxis. At the end of the trial, echocardiographic progression was significantly more likely in the control group (8.2% vs 0.8%, p < 0.001, NNT = 14).
Management of heart failure: standard therapies (e.g., diuretics, ACE inhibitors) may be helpful but are contraindicated during pregnancy.

Authors of a systematic review found that use of diuretics, ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers for left ventricular dysfunction, and beta-blockers and ivabradine for rate control in mitral stenosis, reduced symptoms but there was no evidence that they altered the natural history of disease or need for surgery.

In an RCT including 4565 patients with atrial fibrillation and echocardiographically-documented RHD (mean age 50.5 years, 72.3% women), dose-adjusted vitamin K antagonists were superior to rivaroxaban with respect to a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, or death. A higher incidence of death occurred in the rivaroxaban group with a restricted mean survival time of 1608 days vs. 1680 days with a vitamin K antagonist; difference -72 days (95% CI -117 to -28).
Surgery may be necessary in cases of medically-unresponsive severe heart failure due to mitral (most commonly) or aortic insufficiency.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies of RHD, including 2,410 mitral valve (MV) repairs and 3,598 replacements, found both lower operative mortality and lower long-term mortality with repair vs. replacement (3.2% vs 4.3%; OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50-0.92; I2 0% and 5.0% vs 16%; OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.30–0.56; I2 0%). Re-operation rates, however, were higher with MV repair (12.4% vs 5.4%; OR 2.75, 95% CI 1.57–4.82; I2 65%, although with greater uncertainty.

In a case series of 1731 consecutive patients undergoing MV surgery for rheumatic MV disease, 283 patients (16.3%) died and 256 patients (14.8%) experienced valve-related complications during the 130.9 ± 27.7-month follow-up period. Propensity-score matching produced 188 pairs of repair or valve replacement. Comparing these patients, there was no significant difference in mortality or reoperation risk, although risk of composite valve-related complications was significantly lower in the repair group (HR 0.57; 95% CI 0.33-0.99) primarily due to fewer hemorrhagic events.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs with 553 patients with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis concluded that there were no meaningful differences between percutaneous transvenous mitral commissurotomy compared to surgical commissurotomy for restenosis or re-intervention, symptoms as inferred from immediate postprocedural mitral valve area, or incidence of postprocedural severe mitral regurgitation.
Active carditis at the time of surgery is a predictor of mortality and valve failure.
ARF with carditis and residual heart (valvular) disease: continue treatment at least 10 years from last episode and at least until age 40 years, sometimes lifelong.
ARF with carditis but no residual valvular disease: continue treatment for 10 years or well into adulthood.
ARF without carditis: continue treatment for 5 years or until age 21 years, whichever is longer.
Hospitalize almost all patients for cardiac monitoring and supportive care.

Consider consultation with infectious disease and cardiology consultants, especially if severe carditis with heart failure is present for assistance with diagnosis, treatment, and long-term follow-up.
Heart failure refractory to medical management may require surgical intervention; coordinate care with cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery consultants.

Infective endocarditis (IE) is diagnosed using the modified Duke Criteria, including transthoracic echocardiography or transesophogeal echocardiography if high risk or difficult imaging, and 3 sets of blood cultures.

Treatment options for uncomplicated cases include both aqueous crystalline penicillin G and ceftriaxone for 4 weeks PLUS a 2-week course of gentamicin in those with rapid response to therapy and no underlying renal disease treatment. For patients who can’t tolerate penicillin or ceftriaxone, a 4-week course of vancomycin is recommended. Consultation with an infectious disease specialist is also recommended.

The incidence of atrial fibrillation in patients with RHD is 4.8%, 11.4%, 13.2%, and 30.8% at 1, 2, 5, and 10-years follow-up, respectively, based on 83 studies reporting data from 75,637 participants with RHD in 42 countries. In this study, AF was associated with increased age (mean difference 9.5 years, 95% CI 7.8-1.3), advanced heart failure (OR 4.4, 95% CI 2.1-9.3), and tricuspid valve involvement (OR 4.0, 95% CI 3.0-5.3) in addition to other clinical and laboratory parameters.
ECG is recommended for nearly all patients.
Consider ECG and cardiac monitoring (for early detection of heart block, atrial arrhythmias), and chest X-ray.
Monitor serum aspirin levels and liver enzymes closely if using salicylates.
Prognosis ultimately depends on severity of valvular disease, which is related to the extent of carditis in the initial episode and number of recurrences. C
Follow-up and testing are based on the type of valvular disease, as per AHA guidelines. C
ARF attack rate following an episode of untreated GAS pharyngitis is up to 3%.
It has been estimated that, globally, 60% of all ARF cases result in RHD and 1.5% of these patients die each year.

In a 2-year follow-up of 3343 patients from 25 centers in 14 low and middle-income countries, the mortality rate was 116.3/1000 patient-years in the first year and 65.4/1000 patient-years in the second year with a median age at death of 28.7 years.
Mitral and aortic regurgitation are the most common sequelae.
Arthritis and chorea are almost always self-limited with no chronic effects.
Stroke incidence in patients with RHD is estimated at 4.5/100 patient years in the US.

In an Australian registry study of 572 individuals with ARF and 1248 with RHD in 1997 to 2013 (94.9% Indigenous), both ARF recurrence and progression to RHD was highest in the first year following the initial episode (incidence 3.7 per 100 person-years and 35.9 per 100 person-years, respectively). Likewise, RHD complications were most common in the first year following RHD and included, per 100 person-years, heart failure, 9.09; atrial fibrillation, 4.70; endocarditis, 1.00; and stroke, 0.58. Mortality was higher among Indigenous patients with RHD (hazard ratio, 6.55; 95% CI 2.45-17.51).

In a study of 227 confirmed cases of latent RHD in children in Uganda with median follow-up of 2.3 years, almost half (47.6%) of those with moderate-to-severe definite RHD had echocardiographic progression (including 2 deaths) and 9.5% had echocardiographic regression. Among children with mild-definite and borderline RHD, 26% and 9.8%, respectively, showed echocardiographic progression and 45.2% and 46.3% had echocardiographic improvement.

The estimated pooled prevalence rate for progression of latent RHD was 5% per year (95% CI 2-8) based on a meta-analysis of 12 studies of school-aged children from 9 countries. Eight studies evaluated the progression of borderline latent RHD and reported an estimated pooled prevalence of 2%/year (95% CI 0-4).
Treatment of GAS throat infection reduces risk of RF by 70% to 80%.
Primary and secondary prophylaxis have been very effective in reducing RHD incidence and mortality (e.g., US deaths from ARF and RHD in 2004: 3248. In 1950, there were 15,000 deaths).

In the screening study noted above, 7.5% (95% CI 1.5-17.6) of the cases of RHD identified on echocardiographic screening progressed, while 60.7% (95% CI 42.4-77.5) of cases remained stable over the course of follow-up. Of cases with borderline RHD, 11.3% (95% CI 6.9-16.5) progressed to definite RHD.
Extent of residual valve disease depends on severity of initial episode of carditis; progressive damage occurs with recurrent attacks if not receiving prophylaxis.
Ultimate prognosis is determined by extent and location of valvular disease.

In one retrospective study of 253 patients with rheumatic mitral valve repair, freedom from valve failure at 5 and 10 years was 91.4% and 81.5% and freedom from reoperation for rheumatic valves at 5 and 10 years was 98.4%. The only significant independent predictor of reoperation was presence of residual mitral regurgitation greater than 2+.
Long-term follow-up is based on presence and severity of rheumatic (valvular) heart disease.
Tenascin-C, an extracellular matrix tissue remodeling glycoprotein, may be useful as a prognostic biomarker for rheumatic carditis.
Cardiology consultation is recommended for assistance with clinical and echocardiographic monitoring as per American College of Cardiology/AHA Guidelines.
In one study of patients with asymptomatic rheumatic mitral stenosis, two-dimensional atrial systolic strain imaging on echocardiography predicted subsequent atrial fibrillation.

Using an international registry of consecutive pregnant women with RHD, 273 with mitral stenosis with or without mitral regurgitation and 117 with isolated MR, 1 patient with severe MS died and 23.1% were hospitalized, primarily for heart failure. Data were available for about half the women at 6-months postpartum and 3 additional women died; one with severe MS, 1 with moderate MS, 1 with moderate to severe MR.
In pregnant women with ARF and class III or IV heart failure due to mitral stenosis, percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty is a safe alternative to surgery.
ARF is less common in children under 5 years; young children may present with more severe carditis and more often with erythema marginatum.

feature.caption: Revision of the Jones Criteria for Diagnosis of Acute Rheumatic Fever. (If accompanied by evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection, the presence of two major or of one major and two minor manifestations indicates a high probability of acute rheumatic fever.)
feature.feature_body:
Low Risk Populations* Moderate to High-Risk Populations
Major Manifestations
• Carditis (clinical or subclinical) • Carditis (clinical or subclinical)
• Polyarthritis • Mono, polyarthritis or polyarthralgia†
• Chorea • Chorea
• Erythema marginatum • Erythema marginatum
• Subcutaneous nodules • Subcutaneous nodules
Minor Manifestations
• Polyarthralgia, fever (≥38.5°C) • Monoarthralgia, fever (≥38°C)
• ESR ≥60 mm in the first hour and/or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL • ESR ≥60 mm in the first hour and/or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dL
• Prolonged PR interval‡
• Prolonged PR interval‡
Supporting Evidence of Antecedent Group A Streptococcal Infection
• Positive GAS throat culture for any patient
• Rapid streptococcal antigen test for a child whose clinical presentation suggests a high pretest probability of streptococcal pharyngitis
• Elevated or rising streptococcal antibody titer or other streptococcal antibodies (anti-DNASE B)
Abbreviations: CRP, C-reactive protein; ESR, erythrocyte sedimentation rate *Low-risk populations are those with ARF incidence ≤2 per 100,000 school-aged children or all-age rheumatic heart disease prevalence of ≤1 per 1000 population per year. †If no other causes ‡after accounting for age variability (unless carditis is a major criterion) FROM: Gewitz MH, Baltimore RS, Tani LY, Sable CA, Shulman ST, et al., American Heart Association Committee on Rheumatic Fever, Endocarditis, and Kawasaki Disease of the Council on Cardiovascular Disease in the Young. Revision of the Jones Criteria for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever in the era of Doppler echocardiography: a scientific statement from the American Heart Association. Circulation 2015;131:1806-1818.
